prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Instance segmentation is a critical component for Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) systems, enabling precise interaction between virtual elements and the physical world. However, executing this task on wearable, resource-constrained devices (such as AR glasses) presents a significant bottleneck. The high-resolution sensors required for immersive video capture generate massive data volumes, causing conventional segmentation algorithms to suffer from high processing latency. This delay degrades the user experience by breaking real-time responsiveness. Current approaches waste computational resources by processing the entire field of view with uniform fidelity, failing to account for the fact that users focus their visual attention on very small regions at any given moment.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can achieve substantial computational efficiency without compromising perceived quality by mimicking the physiological mechanism of human foveated vision. We propose that segmentation should not be a global operation but a localized one, triggered and guided by the user's real-time gaze.

Our core intuition rests on two pillars:
1.  **Spatial Efficiency:** By restricting high-fidelity segmentation exclusively to the "Instance of Interest" (IOI) aligned with the user's gaze, we can ignore the vast majority of the peripheral background.
2.  **Temporal Efficiency:** By exploiting human eye behavior—specifically "saccades" (rapid eye movements) and "fixations"—we can skip processing during moments of visual blur and reuse results during moments of stability.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We aim to develop a two-tiered framework: a neural network designed for gaze-contingent processing, and a temporal control algorithm to manage when that network is executed.

**1. Gaze-Aware Neural Network (FSNet)**
We propose a "plug-and-play" neural architecture that accepts a high-resolution image and a gaze coordinate as inputs.
*   **Saliency-Guided Sampling:** Instead of uniformly downsampling the input image (which loses detail) or processing the full resolution (which is too slow), we will implement a learnable sampling layer. This layer will use the gaze coordinate to generate a distortion map, preserving high resolution around the foveal region while aggressively compressing the periphery.
*   **Dual-Branch Output:** Unlike standard segmentation that categorizes every pixel in an image, our network will focus solely on the IOI. We will split the architecture into two lightweight branches:
    *   **Mask Branch:** Generates a binary mask separating the specific object under the gaze from the background.
    *   **Class Branch:** Predicts the semantic category of that single object.
*   **Training Strategy:** We will employ a training scheme that freezes the segmentation backbone while learning the optimal sampling distortion, followed by fine-tuning the segmentation heads. We will design the loss function to weigh the IOI pixels significantly higher than the background to prevent the network from ignoring small, focused objects.

**2. Temporal Control Framework (FovealSeg)**
To further reduce redundancy, we will wrap the network in a temporal logic controller based on eye dynamics:
*   **Saccade Detection:** We will monitor the velocity of gaze shifts. If the eye is moving rapidly (a saccade), we assume the user is experiencing "saccadic blur" and perceptual suppression. During this phase, we will halt segmentation entirely to save power.
*   **Fixation and Reuse:** When the gaze stabilizes (fixation), we will compare the current video frame to the previous one. If the pixel difference is minimal and the gaze remains within the bounds of the previously detected object, we will bypass the network and simply reuse the previous segmentation mask. The heavy neural network will be triggered *only* when the visual scene changes significantly or the gaze shifts to a new target.

## Expected Contribution
This project aims to bridge the gap between heavy computer vision tasks and lightweight edge hardware. By introducing a biologically inspired "foveated" processing pipeline, we expect to demonstrate that high-resolution instance segmentation is feasible in real-time AR environments. The theoretical contribution lies in effectively coupling human oculomotor behavior (saccadic suppression and fixation) with deep learning architectures to dynamically allocate computational resources where they matter most.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the Foveated Instance Segmentation (FSNet) and the broader FovealSeg framework. The experiments were designed to measure segmentation accuracy (IoU), computational efficiency (FLOPs), and processing latency in simulated Augmented Reality (AR) environments.

*   **Hardware and Simulation:**
    *   We simulated hardware performance using the GPU simulation tool GPGPU-Sim.
    *   The simulation was configured to model the **Jetson Orin NX**, a standard edge GPU for AR/VR devices.
    *   Eye-tracking latency was modeled at 5–10 milliseconds with sampling rates up to 120 Hz.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Cityscapes:** Urban scene understanding (20,000 images, 19 classes).
    *   **ADE20K:** Scene parsing (30,000 images, 31 classes).
    *   **LVIS:** Large vocabulary instance segmentation (100,000 images, 50 classes).
    *   **Aria Everyday Activities:** Egocentric data from VR headsets (60,000 images, 100 classes).
    *   *Note:* Gaze traces from the Aria dataset were incorporated into Cityscapes for temporal evaluation, as Cityscapes lacks native gaze data.

*   **Model Architecture Details:**
    *   **Saliency DNN:** A lightweight 3-layer U-Net.
    *   **Classification DNN ($S_{cls}$):** Pre-trained MobileNetV2.
    *   **Segmentation DNNs ($S_{seg}$):** We evaluated four backbones:
        1.  DeepLabV3
        2.  HRNet
        3.  SegFormer-B4
        4.  SegFormer-B5
    *   **Input Resolutions for FSNet Experiments:**
        *   Cityscapes: Downsampled to $64 \times 128$.
        *   ADE20K: Downsampled to $80 \times 80$.
        *   LVIS: Downsampled to $80 \times 80$.
        *   Aria: Downsampled to $180 \times 180$.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Avg (Uniform Subsampling):** Uniformly subsampled input processed by the segmentation network.
    *   **LTD (Learn-to-Downsample):** A learnable downsampling approach performing segmentation on the entire frame.
    *   **ND (No Downsample):** Conventional segmentation on full-resolution ($640 \times 640$) images.
    *   **NS (No Skip):** FovealSeg framework processing downsampled images ($64 \times 64$) but without the frame-skipping (gaze reuse) mechanism.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **IoU:** Intersection over Union over the Instance of Interest (IOI) within the full-resolution test input.
    *   **IoU':** Intersection over Union over the IOI within the subsampled version of the input.
    *   **FLOPs:** Floating Point Operations (Normalized).
    *   **Latency:** Processing time in milliseconds (ms).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Training Strategy:** Alternate training. Step 1: Segmentation components frozen, Saliency DNN trained. Step 2: Saliency DNN frozen, Segmentation network fine-tuned.
    *   **Loss Function:** Combination of Dice loss and weighted Focal loss (weighted by the inverse area of the IOI vs non-IOI regions).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Model Latency and Speedup (from Figure 3 and Text)**
*   Processing semantic segmentation on a full input size of $640 \times 640$ resulted in latencies exceeding 300 ms on the simulated edge GPU.
*   SegFormer-B5 specifically experienced delays of over a second (approx. 5,280 ms) at full resolution ($640 \times 640$).
*   Reducing input size to $64 \times 64$ dramatically lowered latency.
*   We observed the following speedups when comparing $640 \times 640$ to $64 \times 64$ inputs:
    *   **Seg-B5:** 96x speedup (5,280 ms down to 55 ms).
    *   **Seg-B4:** 88x speedup (3,784 ms down to 43 ms).
    *   **DeepLab:** 76x speedup (344 ms down to 5 ms).
    *   **HRNet-w32:** 84x speedup (668 ms down to 8 ms).
    *   **HRNet-w48:** 90x speedup (4,258 ms down to 47 ms).

**Gaze Behavior Analysis (from Figure 4 and Text)**
*   **Gaze Reuse:** We found that 95% of frames within a designated segment exhibited a gaze location difference below 0.1 (normalized).
*   **Image Similarity:** We observed that 35% of consecutive frame pairs had a pixel-wise difference of less than 0.037.
*   **Thresholding:** A threshold of 0.1 for gaze difference effectively grouped locations within a fixation phase; values above this indicated saccades. A pixel difference threshold of 0.037 was sufficient to group similar frames.

**Computational Efficiency / FLOPs (from Figure 7)**
*   We normalized FLOPs relative to the FovealSeg framework (set to 1.0).
*   **FovealSeg vs. No Skip (NS):** The NS baseline (downsampling without frame skipping) required between 1.28x and 1.96x more FLOPs than FovealSeg, depending on the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ thresholds used.
*   **FovealSeg vs. No Downsample (ND):** The ND baseline (full resolution) required vastly more computation. Specifically:
    *   For Seg-B5 (thresholds 0.05/0.005), ND required **73x** more FLOPs.
    *   For DeepLab (thresholds 0.05/0.01), ND required **49x** more FLOPs.
    *   For Seg-B5 (thresholds 0.1/0.005), ND required **75x** more FLOPs.
    *   For DeepLab (thresholds 0.1/0.01), ND required **44x** more FLOPs.
*   Overall, leveraging gaze saccades and fixations eliminated redundant computations, achieving up to a **1.96x reduction** in FLOPs compared to downsampling alone, and up to a **75x reduction** compared to full-resolution processing.

**General Findings**
*   **Accuracy:** FSNet consistently outperformed all baselines (Avg, LTD) across all datasets. We observed an improvement of at least 0.14 in IoU and 0.15 in IoU' compared to the Avg method.
*   **Robustness:** The gap between IoU and IoU' was consistently small ($< 0.02$), indicating the training strategy effectively handled both upsampling and downsampling.
*   **Importance of Gaze:** Removing gaze information (substituting with random noise) caused a drastic performance drop of over 0.3 IoU (Table 5).
*   **Kernel Size:** Increasing the Gaussian kernel size from 17 to 33 improved performance, as it placed more emphasis on the saliency region (Table 4).
*   **Latency Impact:** The latency reduction provided by FovealSeg (84ms vs 1860ms for SegFormer-B5) significantly improved temporal alignment between gaze and segmentation mask, reducing the delay artifacts observed in the baseline.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables

```latex
    Method & Frobnability \\
```


## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Instance segmentation is a critical component for Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) systems, enabling the precise recognition and separation of virtual and physical elements. However, this task imposes severe computational overhead, particularly given the high-resolution input (e.g., 12MP sensors) required by modern head-mounted displays. Running standard segmentation algorithms on resource-constrained edge devices results in significant processing latency (often exceeding 300ms), which shatters the real-time responsiveness required for an immersive user experience (10-20ms latency target). Current approaches that process entire image frames or batches of consecutive frames are fundamentally inefficient because they waste computation on peripheral regions that the user is not observing.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a **Foveated Instance Segmentation (FovealSeg)** framework. Our core hypothesis is that by leveraging real-time gaze tracking data, we can restrict high-resolution segmentation inference exclusively to the **Instance of Interest (IOI)**—the specific object geographically aligned with the user's foveal vision. Furthermore, we hypothesize that by exploiting human eye behavior—specifically the insensitivity of vision during **saccades** (rapid eye movements) and the temporal stability during **fixations**—we can skip processing or reuse segmentation masks across multiple frames, drastically reducing computational load without degrading the perceived visual experience.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a two-stage system: **FSNet**, a deep neural network for single-frame foveated segmentation, and **FovealSeg**, a temporal framework managing execution across video frames.

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of Saliency-Guided Downsampling
We will define image downsampling as a transformation of the original image $F \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ into a smaller representation $\hat{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times C}$. This will be controlled by mapping functions $G^h$ and $G^w$ which map normalized coordinates from $\hat{F}$ back to $F$.

To make this process differentiable and gaze-aware, we will employ a **saliency-based sampling layer**. We will train a Saliency DNN, denoted as $D_{\theta}(.)$, which takes the full image $F$ and normalized coordinates $(i, j)$ to produce a density score map. The mapping functions will be computed as a weighted sum using a Gaussian kernel $k_{\sigma}$:

$$ G^{h}(i, j) = \frac{\sum_{i', j'} D_{\theta}(i', j') k_{\sigma}\left( \left( \frac{i}{h}, \frac{j}{w} \right), \left( \frac{i'}{H}, \frac{j'}{W} \right) \right) i'}{\sum_{i', j'} D_{\theta}(i', j') k_{\sigma}\left( \left( \frac{i}{h}, \frac{j}{w} \right), \left( \frac{i'}{H}, \frac{j'}{W} \right) \right)} $$

$$ G^{w}(i, j) = \frac{\sum_{i', j'} D_{\theta}(i', j') k_{\sigma}\left( \left( \frac{i}{h}, \frac{j}{w} \right), \left( \frac{i'}{H}, \frac{j'}{W} \right) \right) j'}{\sum_{i', j'} D_{\theta}(i', j') k_{\sigma}\left( \left( \frac{i}{h}, \frac{j}{w} \right), \left( \frac{i'}{H}, \frac{j'}{W} \right) \right)} $$

where $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the kernel. This allows the network to "zoom in" on relevant areas dynamically.

### 2. FSNet Architecture Design
FSNet will integrate gaze data directly into the network structure.

**Gaze Map Construction:**
We will generate a gaze map $N$ based on the user's gaze location $(u, v)$. This map represents the normalized inverse distance to the gaze point, concatenated channel-wise to the input image. Each element $N[i, j]$ is defined as:
$$ N[i, j] = 1 - \frac{\sqrt{(i-u)^2 + (j-v)^2}}{d_{max}} $$
where $d_{max} = \sqrt{H^2 + W^2}$ is the normalization factor.

**Dual-Branch Segmentation Network:**
Unlike standard segmentation which outputs dense pixel-wise class maps, FSNet will output only the IOI information. The downsampled input $\hat{F}$ will be fed into a segmentation network $S$ split into two branches:
1.  **Mask Branch ($S_{seg}$):** Produces a binary map $Y_{bm} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times 1}$ identifying the IOI region (1 for IOI, 0 for background).
2.  **Classification Branch ($S_{cls}$):** Produces a class vector $Y_{cls} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times 1}$.

The final segmentation label $Y$ is the outer product of these branches:
$$ Y = Y_{cls} \otimes Y_{bm} $$

**Loss Function Design:**
To handle the class imbalance caused by small IOIs, we will weigh the loss by the inverse area of the IOI. The total loss $\mathbb{L}_{tot}$ will combine Dice loss and weighted Focal loss between the subsampled ground truth $Y'_{gt}$ and predicted mask $Y_{cm}$:
$$ \mathbb{L}_{tot} = L_{dice}(Y'_{gt}, Y_{cm}) + \lambda L_{focal}(Y'_{gt}, Y_{cm}) $$

### 3. FovealSeg Temporal Framework
We will implement an algorithm to manage inference across video frames, utilizing specific criteria to skip redundant computations.

**Saccade Detection:**
We will calculate the squared difference between the current gaze location $g_t$ and the buffered location $g_{last}$. If $|g_t - g_{last}|^2 > \alpha$, we classify the movement as a saccade. During saccades, we will **halt segmentation entirely**, exploiting the human visual system's "saccadic blur" (reduced sensitivity).

**Segment Detection and Reuse:**
If no saccade is detected, we check for scene stability.
1.  We compute the pixel-wise difference between the current frame $F^t$ and the segment's initial frame $F^{init}$.
2.  If $\sum |F^t - F^{init}| > \beta$, the scene has changed significantly; we trigger a full execution of FSNet.
3.  If the scene is stable, we check if the current gaze $g_t$ falls within the previously generated IOI mask $M_{last}$. If it does, we **reuse $M_{last}$** without running inference. If not, we run FSNet.

### 4. Training Strategy
We will employ an alternating training strategy:
1.  **Phase 1:** Freeze the segmentation network ($S_{seg}, S_{cls}$) and train only the Saliency DNN to learn optimal downsampling.
2.  **Phase 2:** Freeze the Saliency DNN and fine-tune the segmentation network.

## Expected Contribution
This research aims to theoretically and practically demonstrate that instance segmentation in AR/VR does not require uniform high-resolution processing. By creating a gaze-contingent pipeline, we expect to:
1.  **Reduce Computational Cost:** Achieve orders-of-magnitude reduction in FLOPs by processing only foveated regions.
2.  **Minimize Latency:** Enable real-time performance on edge hardware where standard backbones currently fail.
3.  **Provide a Generalizable Module:** Offer FSNet as a "plug-and-play" module that can act as a frontend for various existing segmentation backbones (e.g., DeepLab, SegFormer, HRNet).

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.

notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.

notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
